name: Testolactone (Teslac)

lead: Testolactone (Teslac) was a prescription aromatase inhibitor approved in the US in 1970 for advanced breast cancer and discontinued in 2008. Bodybuilders have discussed it for limiting estrogen during steroid use, aiming for less water retention and a drier look.

It blocks the aromatase enzyme that converts androgens to estrogens, with a lowering of estradiol that is modest compared with newer drugs. It was also studied in children with precocious puberty and in infertile men; no trial has examined it for appearance.

paras: Medically it was an oral daily drug for postmenopausal breast cancer. It is no longer available, and newer aromatase inhibitors have taken over the roles it was discussed for.
Reported effects include tingling, aches, hair loss, nausea and vomiting, with rarer allergic reactions and edema. It is no longer available for medical use.

angle.text: Testolactone is a discontinued aromatase inhibitor that bodybuilders discussed for limiting estrogen: less conversion of androgens to estrogen means less water retention and a drier look. It was studied for breast cancer, and nothing was tested for looks.

lead: Testolactone, sold as Teslac, is a steroidal first-generation aromatase inhibitor that was used as an anticancer drug for advanced breast cancer in postmenopausal women. It was first approved in the United States in 1970 and was discontinued in 2008.[1]

Because aromatase converts androgens to estrogens, aromatase inhibitors have been of interest in bodybuilding and hormone-optimisation circles for managing estrogen-related effects such as gynecomastia. Testolactone has been described as having been studied in men for infertility, gynecomastia and growth in children, but it is no longer available for medical use and is superseded by later agents.[1][2][3]

The appearance connection runs through estrogen: by lowering estrogen synthesis, aromatase inhibitors can reduce the estrogen drive on male breast tissue, which is why testolactone was examined for gynecomastia (chest appearance) [4], and in children estrogen is involved in bone maturation, so it was used in regimens aimed at slowing early puberty and protecting predicted adult height [5][6][7][8].
No published trial has tested testolactone for appearance outcomes.

paras: Testolactone treated breast cancer in postmenopausal women or women whose ovaries no longer functioned, by lowering estrogen production. It was also used to delay precocious puberty and to treat gynecomastia.[1] Aromatase inhibitors, including testolactone, were examined in men with infertility and abnormal testosterone-to-estradiol ratios.[2][3]

Reviews of gonadotropin-independent precocious puberty describe testolactone, with or without spironolactone, as part of the therapy of testotoxicosis and McCune-Albright syndrome; one review said there was consensus that testolactone or ketoconazole represented optimal management and that testolactone appeared relatively safe and reasonably effective [7][8]. A 2005 review of testotoxicosis says that a combination of spironolactone and testolactone decreased height velocity and improved predicted height [8]. A 1992 series of patients with familial adenomatous polyposis and desmoid tumors included one treated with testolactone [9].

No cosmetic indication exists. Interest in aromatase inhibitors in bodybuilding concerns controlling estrogenic effects of androgens; reviews on aromatase and gynecomastia describe estrogen's role in breast tissue growth in men.[4]

In a review of aromatase and gynecomastia, Delta-1-testolactone is described as the agent on which most published data on aromatase inhibitors in gynecomastia concern; it reduced the size of the breast glandular tissue but did not completely ameliorate the problem, and studies with newer inhibitors were called for [4]. Newer aromatase inhibitors such as anastrozole and letrozole are the ones discussed in modern male-infertility literature [10][11]. Bodybuilding and hormone forums more commonly discuss currently available aromatase inhibitors, such as exemestane, than testolactone [12].

Commonly reported effects included tingling or abnormal skin sensations, limb aches, general discomfort, hair loss, loss of appetite, nausea, redness of the tongue and vomiting. Rarer serious effects included allergic reactions, edema and bone pain.[1]

Testolactone inhibits aromatase, lowering estrogen synthesis; in vitro studies suggest the inhibition may be noncompetitive and irreversible. At a high daily dose in men, estradiol fell by 25 to 50 percent after 6 to 10 days, a smaller reduction than later aromatase inhibitors produce.[1] It has very weak androgen receptor affinity and is classed as a first-generation, steroidal (Type I) inhibitor.[1]
Testolactone is a synthetic 18-oxasteroid, a D-homo analogue of androstenedione in which a six-membered lactone replaces the D ring (formula C19H24O3).[1]

Testolactone was first approved in the United States in 1970 as an antineoplastic and was discontinued in 2008.[1] Later aromatase inhibitors such as anastrozole replaced it in male infertility research.[2]

A 1970 Medical Letter entry on Teslac reflects its introduction as an antineoplastic [13]. A 1981 study examined delta-1-testolactone's effects on the pituitary-testicular axis in oligospermic men, and reviews in 1987 and later evaluated aromatase inhibitors for male infertility [14][15][10]. Estrogen's role in bone growth and maturation in childhood, including a biphasic dose effect, was reviewed in 1997 and underlies interest in aromatase inhibitors for growth in children [16].

Studies in men are about hormones and fertility, not appearance. A 2001 study compared testosterone-to-estradiol ratios in 63 infertile men with controls and tested an oral aromatase inhibitor; a 2002 study evaluated anastrozole in 140 subfertile men, citing earlier improvements with testolactone [2][3]. A 2020 systematic review and meta-analysis of eight articles found that steroidal (testolactone) and nonsteroidal (anastrozole, letrozole) aromatase inhibitors statistically improved all evaluated hormonal parameters in infertile or hypoandrogenic men [10]. A 2012 review says treatment of infertile men with testolactone, anastrozole and letrozole has been associated with increased sperm production, and calls for randomized controlled trials [11].

Children: NIH-registered trials examined testolactone in LHRH-resistant precocious puberty in girls (100 participants, from 1982), in boys with precocious puberty (80 participants, from 1985) and in a three-drug regimen for congenital adrenal hyperplasia (66 participants, from 1995) [5][17][18]. A 2000 study reported that flutamide, testolactone and reduced hydrocortisone maintained normal growth in children with CAH [6].
Gynecomastia: a 1999 review states that most published data on aromatase inhibition in gynecomastia concern testolactone [4].
No studies were found testing testolactone for muscle or other appearance goals in healthy people.
